html:
In 1910 a shop called Rairaiken opened in Asakusa, a lively district of Tokyo, and served Chinese style noodle soup to Japanese customers. It is often named as the first ramen shop.

Its owner, Ozaki Kan'ichi, hired Cantonese cooks from the Chinatown of Yokohama. They made wheat noodles with alkaline water, which gives them their bite and yellow colour, in a soy flavoured pork and chicken broth. The dish was cheap and filling and caught on among workers. At first it was called Shina soba, Chinese noodles.

After the Second World War, cheap American wheat flour, returning soldiers who had eaten noodles in China, and street stalls made ramen everyday food. Regional styles grew up: miso in Sapporo, pork bone broth in Fukuoka. In 1958 Momofuku Ando invented instant noodles, which took a version of the dish worldwide. Ramen is now one of the best known Japanese foods abroad, though its roots are Chinese.
